title: From best cook to menu designer

beats.say: Why do some excellent engineers stop getting promoted? Because the job changes, not just the skill.

show.sub: Senior to staff is a change of role

beats.say: Think of a restaurant. A senior engineer is the best cook. Give them an order, and the dish comes out perfect.
A staff engineer is closer to the person who designs the menu. They notice customers keep complaining about slow dinners, and decide that is the problem worth fixing.
They also write the recipe book, so every kitchen makes the sauce the same way. And they guide other cooks without being their boss.

check.q: In the restaurant picture, what best describes the staff engineer?
opts: The fastest cook on the line
Someone who decides which problem to fix and writes the recipe others follow
The manager who assigns every order
A cook who works only on their own dish
check.why: Staff work is about finding the right problem and shaping how many teams work, not just cooking faster.

work: Write down one problem you noticed that nobody asked you to solve.
Ask a senior colleague how they chose what to work on last quarter.

title: Project, domain, strategy: how scope grows

beats.say: Five teams report active users, and you get five different numbers. Who fixes that?
A senior engineer fixes their own pipeline. A staff engineer notices the pattern and defines the real problem: no single definition exists.

show.title: Fix a *pipeline* or fix the domain

beats.say: Then they write a design document, because documents decide what gets built. Other senior engineers read it and execute, with no formal authority needed, because the argument is sound.
The time horizon stretches too. Seniors plan a quarter, about three months. Staff write strategy for two or three years, and lead migrations that long.

check.q: Five teams compute active users five different ways. What is the staff-level move?
opts: Fix your own team's number and move on
Define one shared metric in a design doc and get teams to adopt it
Ask a manager to order everyone to match
Build a sixth dashboard
check.why: Staff work defines the cross-team problem and uses a document to give others one definition to build on.

work: Pick one metric at work with competing definitions and list who computes each.
Draft a one page problem statement before proposing any solution.

title: Fixing a class of failures, and the traps

beats.say: You fixed the same outage three times. Why is that a warning sign at staff level?

show.sub: Fixing incidents is the senior habit

beats.say: Because staff owns the whole class of failure. After the second one, you ask what makes it impossible: a schema check, a quota, a runbook turned into automation. Then you attach a reliability or cost number to it.

Watch for common traps. Becoming the hero who does everything, so you are the bottleneck. Writing a document nobody reviewed, so nobody follows it. Or drifting so far from code that your designs stop being realistic.

show.title: Staff traps
items: Hero mode: you become the bottleneck
Unreviewed doc: no buy-in, no adoption
No coding: designs lose touch with reality

check.q: The same pipeline fails for the same reason a second time. What should a staff engineer do?
opts: Fix it faster and write a better apology
Add a guardrail that makes that class of failure impossible and track a target
Wait for a third time to be sure
Assign it to the newest engineer
check.why: Staff ownership means removing the class of incident, with a measurable reliability or cost target, not just repairing instances.

work: Review last quarter's incidents and group them by root cause class.
Share your next design doc with reviewers before you build, not after.

title: Choosing what is worth your years

beats.say: In the hiring manager round they ask: how do you choose what to work on? What is a strong answer?

Rank problems by impact on money, risk, or speed, against the effort. A migration that saves two million dollars a year but needs eighteen months of five engineers may lose to a small fix this quarter.
Say no to your own pet projects too. A new standard nobody asked for costs adoption effort. Prefer the boring option when the pain is small.

show.title: When not to lead a big change

beats.say: Prepare three stories: scope across teams, influence without authority, and a decision with a cost you could measure.

check.q: A migration saves two million dollars a year but takes five engineers eighteen months, while a small fix removes most of the pain in a quarter. What is the best reasoning?
opts: Always pick the larger saving
Compare impact against effort and risk, and often take the small fix first
Avoid anything that costs engineers
Let the loudest team decide
check.why: Architects weigh impact against effort, risk and adoption cost. A cheap fix can beat a bigger but slower prize.

work: Write a ranked list of your candidate projects with impact, effort and risk.
Prepare three stories with numbers: scope, influence, and cost.

title: Three documents that settle decisions

beats.say: Why do the best engineers write so much? Because a decision nobody wrote down gets argued again, and again, and again.
Think of a family road trip. A design doc is the route plan you show everyone before leaving. It says why you are going, the roads you rejected, and what you do if the car breaks down.
An architecture decision record is a sticky note on the fridge. One page. We took the coast road because of the ferry. Two years later, nobody has to guess why.

show.title: Decision record
items: The good and the bad it brings

beats.say: A technical strategy is the whole year's travel plan. It names a few big destinations and the trips you are skipping. A plan that skips nothing is only a wish list.

check.q: What is the main job of an architecture decision record?
opts: Explain why a choice was made, long after the people have moved on
List every task for the next sprint
Replace the design doc for large projects
check.why: It is a one-page memory of context, decision and consequences, so nobody has to guess why the system looks the way it does.

work: Find one decision in your team nobody can explain and write a one-page record for it.
Next time you plan a project, write down what you are deliberately not doing.

title: Anatomy of a design doc people approve

beats.say: What goes into a design doc that people actually approve?

Open with the problem, using numbers. For example, the nightly load takes six hours and misses the nine a.m. dashboard deadline twice a week. Then goals, and non-goals: what you are deliberately not doing.

show.title: Start here
items: Context: why now, who is hurt, with numbers
Non-goals: what we will not do

beats.say: Next comes the proposal, with a diagram, data model and interfaces. Then at least two alternatives, each with a reason why not. Without alternatives, reviewers assume you never looked.
Finish with risks, rollout with rollback, cost including the cost of doing nothing, and open questions. Lead with the conclusion on page one, so a busy reader can answer yes or no.

show.title: Close with
items: Risks and how you would know

check.q: Why must a design doc include at least two alternatives with reasons for rejecting them?
opts: To make the document longer
To show the proposal was chosen, not just the first idea
Because the template requires exactly three options
check.why: Alternatives prove you explored the space. Reviewers then trust the proposal and can challenge specific trade-offs.

work: Rewrite your last proposal's first paragraph so it states the conclusion and one number.
Add a cost-of-doing-nothing line to your next design doc.

title: Why good designs still get rejected

beats.say: Why do design docs fail even when the design is good?

First failure: fake alternatives. If the other options are strawmen, a sceptic spots it and distrusts everything else. Second: a vague problem. Pipelines are slow cannot be checked. Six hours, twice late a week, can.

show.title: Doc failures
items: Sections reviewers cannot answer yes or no

beats.say: Decision records rot when nobody writes the bad consequences. Record both sides. Example: Iceberg over Delta for multi-engine reads; consequence, we run our own compaction. Never edit old records. Mark them superseded and add a new one.
Last, show the doc first to your most sceptical reviewer, privately. Their objections cost ten minutes now, instead of a week in the open review.

check.q: An old ADR is now wrong because the team changed direction. What should you do?
opts: Edit it to match the new decision
Delete it to avoid confusion
Mark it superseded and write a new ADR linking to it
check.why: The history of why you chose then, and why you changed, is the value of the record. Rewriting it destroys that.

work: Add a consequences section listing at least one bad outcome to every ADR you write.
Send your next draft privately to the harshest reviewer before the group review.

title: When to write, when not to, and what to cut

beats.say: When should you not write a full design doc?
Skip it for work that is cheap to reverse, like a two day change behind a flag. A short ADR is enough. Heavy documents for small choices slow the team and teach people to ignore them.
Write the full doc when a change is costly to undo, like a new lake format or a migration touching forty pipelines. Its cost section covers build, run, and the cost of doing nothing.

A strategy covers one to three years: where we are, with data, the few big bets, what we stop doing, and how we measure progress. If nothing is stopped, you have not chosen. Pick the biggest cost, and say no to the rest.

check.q: Which sign most clearly shows a technical strategy is weak?
opts: It is only three pages long
It lists priorities but stops nothing
It includes metrics for progress
check.why: Strategy is choice. If no work is dropped or declined, it is a wish list that spreads the team thin.

work: Create a simple rule for your team: reversible changes get an ADR, costly ones get a full doc.
Review your current roadmap and name two things you would explicitly stop.

title: Leading without being the boss

beats.say: How do you change what ten teams do when none of them report to you?
Think of a town with a dangerous crossroads. You are not the mayor. Shouting gets nowhere. But if you count the accidents and put the numbers on a big board, people start to see the problem.
Next, ask the shopkeepers who will object what worries them, and fix the plan. Then paint a safe crosswalk, so walking the right way is the easiest way. Nobody needs persuading to use it.

show.title: Win people, then make it easy
items: Fold their worries into the plan
Paint the crosswalk: the easy path

beats.say: Finally, let a neighbour cut the ribbon and take the credit. Influence means people want to follow, not that they must.

check.q: In the crossroads story, what is the best first move for someone with no authority?
opts: Demand the mayor build a roundabout
Count the accidents and show everyone
Paint your own crosswalk quietly
Wait until people complain
check.why: Making the problem visible with data turns a personal opinion into a shared fact, which is the base for any influence without authority.

work: Pick one pain you keep complaining about and find a number that measures it.
List who would object to your idea and ask each one what worries them.
Name one person who can present your next idea instead of you.

title: The influence playbook, step by step

beats.say: Why does nobody fix a pipeline problem that fails forty runs every week?

Because nobody sees it. Build a dashboard first. Show failed runs, the engineer hours lost, and the cost. Or list the five different revenue definitions finance is using. Data turns an opinion into a fact.
Then write a short design doc. Send it early to the three people most likely to say no. Their objections go into the doc, so they become co-authors, not blockers.
Last, make the right thing easy. A template or library that sets up a pipeline in ten minutes beats a month of meetings. Adoption stops depending on persuasion.

show.title: Make the right thing the *easy* thing

check.q: Why send a design doc early to the people most likely to object?
opts: It lets you claim they were consulted
It shortens the review meeting
Their objections improve the design and they become supporters
It avoids needing any data
check.why: Early feedback is cheap to absorb. Objectors who shaped the doc have ownership in it, so they are less likely to block it later.

work: Build one chart of failed runs or cost before you pitch your next change.
Share your next draft with your toughest critic before the review.
Turn a repeated manual setup into a template others can copy.

title: Why good advice sometimes changes nothing

beats.say: Why do some architects give great advice and still change nothing?
A common failure is presenting a finished design on review day. People feel ambushed and say no. Share drafts early, when changing your mind is still cheap.

Mentoring needs structure. Hold regular one to ones. Hand over a stretch piece with a safety net, like you reviewing the design before build. Review designs, not only code, because design mistakes cost far more to fix.

show.title: Mentor deliberately
items: Stretch work with a safety net

beats.say: When you lose an argument, disagree and commit honestly. State your data, accept the decision, support it fully, and write down what evidence would reopen it. Quiet sabotage destroys trust.

check.q: You lost a design argument. What does honest disagree and commit look like?
opts: Comply but let the project slip to prove your point
Keep arguing in every meeting
Support it fully and record what evidence would reopen the decision
Escalate to a manager after the decision
check.why: Committing means real support. Recording the reopen trigger keeps the decision evidence-based without turning disagreement into sabotage.

work: Share your next design as a rough draft a week before any review.
Give a junior a stretch task and agree when you will check in.
Write a reopen condition in the decision log next time you lose a debate.

title: When influence is the wrong tool

beats.say: When is persuasion the wrong tool, and a rule the right one?

show.sub: Choose on the cost of being wrong

beats.say: Paved paths cost real engineering time, maybe two people for a quarter. Build one only when many teams repeat the same work. For one team, a conversation is cheaper.

Influence does not scale through you. If every design needs your review, you become the bottleneck. Train senior engineers to run reviews, give them the presentation, and sponsor them for visible work.
For risks like security or data privacy, choose a firm policy over persuasion. Mandates are fast but breed resentment. Paved paths are slower but stick. Pick by how costly a wrong choice is.

show.title: Mandate or paved path
items: High-risk areas like privacy: firm policy

check.q: When is a firm mandate better than a paved path?
opts: When a wrong choice is costly, such as a privacy or security risk
When only one team has the problem
When you want the team to feel ownership
When you have no time to write a doc
check.why: Mandates are fast and certain, which matters when a mistake is costly. For ordinary choices, paved paths build lasting adoption with less resentment.

work: Count how many teams repeat the same work before proposing a paved path.
List the reviews that only you do and hand one to a senior engineer.
Decide which two risks in your platform deserve a firm policy.

title: The story bank, like a toolbox

beats.say: Why do strong engineers freeze when asked about a time they failed? Because they never practised telling it out loud.

show.text: Why freeze on a question you already lived?

beats.say: Think of a story bank as a toolbox. You do not invent a tool when the job starts. You reach in and pick one. About twelve stories cover almost every question, because questions keep repeating the same themes: conflict, failure, influence, cost.
Each story follows STAR. Situation: what was going on. Task: what was your job. Action: what you did. Result: what changed. Tell it like the plot of a short film, not a diary.
Keep it under three minutes, say I for your part, and finish with a number. People remember numbers.

show.text: Under 3 minutes. Say I. End with a number.

check.q: Why prepare about twelve stories instead of one answer per possible question?
opts: Questions are unlimited, so more is always better
Questions repeat a few themes, so a small bank can be reused
Interviewers ask for exactly twelve stories
Stories should be memorised word for word
check.why: Behavioural questions cluster around a handful of themes such as conflict, failure and influence, so one well-built story can be adapted to several prompts.

work: List ten projects from your career and note which theme each fits
Write one sentence each for situation, task, action and result of your best story
Tell one story aloud to a friend and time it

title: Building stories that fit three minutes

beats.say: How do you squeeze a whole career into twelve stories of under three minutes each?

Start with themes. Influence without authority, big delivery, failure, conflict, ambiguity, raising the bar, cost, mentoring, customer focus, and prioritisation. One story can cover two themes, so twelve stories are enough to cover ten.
Then budget the time. About thirty seconds for situation and task, ninety seconds for action, and forty seconds for result and lesson. Action gets the most time because that is what is scored.
The result needs a number: hours saved, cost cut, incidents down, people affected. Then prepare a follow-up two levels deeper, because interviewers dig two or three times.

check.q: In a three-minute story, which part should get the most time?
opts: Situation, to set the scene fully
Action, what you personally did
Result, repeated for emphasis
Task, to define the goal
check.why: Interviewers score your own decisions and actions, so about ninety seconds should go to what you did and why.

work: Map each of your stories to one or two themes and find the gaps
Add a concrete number to the result of every story
Write two deeper follow-up questions for each story and answer them

title: Why a good story still gets marked down

beats.say: You told a great story and still got marked down. What went wrong?
The most common cause is we. If you say we built it, the interviewer cannot tell what you did, so they have nothing to score. Say I for your part, and name the team honestly for the rest.
Second, failure stories that are secret boasts. A real failure names your mistake, what it cost, and what you changed afterwards. Third, no number and no lesson means no proof.

show.title: Traps
items: Failure that is really a boast

beats.say: Expect the dig. Why that choice? What would you do differently? A thin story falls apart at level three. Amazon scores Leadership Principles in every round, so map each story to a principle.

check.q: Which failure story is strongest?
opts: A deadline slipped because another team was late
You worked a weekend and saved the launch
You made a wrong design call, it cost two days of outages, and you added a review step
You say the failure was being too much of a perfectionist
check.why: A strong failure names your own mistake, its real cost with a number, and a lasting change you made.

work: Rewrite each story replacing we with I where it was your work
Check every failure story for owned mistake, cost and change
Tag each story with the Amazon principles it could prove

title: What staff-level stories must prove

beats.say: At staff level, what is the interviewer really measuring in a story?
Scope and judgment, not effort. They want proof you changed what a team or organisation did, weighed trade-offs, and said no to something important. A heroic weekend fix signals senior, not staff.

Your analyst background is leverage. Defining a metric people trust, or translating between engineers and stakeholders, is what cross-functional means. It appears in sixty-three percent of staff postings.

show.sub: of staff postings ask for cross-functional work

beats.say: There is a trade-off. A polished script sounds fake, a loose story rambles. Memorise the outline and the number, not the sentences. If AI tools are allowed in coding rounds, narrate your approach and verify the output aloud.

show.title: Practice rules
items: Narrate your approach with AI tools

check.q: Why is a story about a heroic weekend fix weak for a staff interview?
opts: It shows too much technical depth
It shows effort but not scope, trade-offs or organisational change
Weekend work is always penalised
It has no situation
check.why: Staff roles are judged on influence and judgment across teams. Individual heroics show execution, not that you changed how others work.

work: Pick your three stories with the widest scope and rehearse those first
Turn one analyst story into a metric-trust or translation story with a number
Practise a coding task with an AI assistant while explaining and checking its output aloud

title: A promise, not a hope

beats.say: Is the revenue table reliable? If your answer is usually, that is a hope, not a promise.
Think of a train timetable. The measurement is how late the train arrives. The promise is nine out of ten trains within five minutes. Everyone can check it.

Data works the same way. Measure how late the table lands. Promise it lands by six in the morning on ninety nine days out of a hundred. The few late days are your allowance for trouble. Spend that allowance, and fixing things comes before new features.

check.q: What turns 'the table is usually fine' into a real reliability promise?
opts: Asking the team to try harder
A measured number with a target, such as on time 99 days in 100
Adding more dashboards
Running the pipeline twice
check.why: A promise needs something measured and a target everyone can check. Effort and extra runs do not give you either.

work: Pick your three most important tables and write down when each should land.
Ask the owner of each how often it landed on time last quarter.

title: Cost is a bill you can read

beats.say: Your cloud bill doubled. Is that bad news or good news?
Picture an electricity bill for a whole apartment block. One total tells you nothing. You need to know which flat uses the most, and the biggest few usually cause most of the bill.

chip.text: Few spenders, most of the bill

beats.say: Then you can switch off lights nobody uses, and run the washing machine less often. And you report cost per person, not just the total. If the block gained twice the residents, a doubled bill is fine. Data teams call this unit cost.

show.title: Read the bill well
items: Report cost per person, not the total
Doubled bill with doubled residents is fine

check.q: Why report cost per person (unit cost) instead of only the total bill?
opts: It makes the bill smaller
It separates growth in use from waste
It removes the need for tags
It is required by the cloud provider
check.why: A bigger total can come from more use. A unit cost shows whether each unit of work got cheaper or dearer.

work: Find out who owns the three largest items on your cloud bill.
Pick one unit, such as cost per terabyte processed, and write it down monthly.

title: SLI, SLO and the error budget

beats.say: How many late days a year is ninety nine percent allowed to have?
Start with the SLI, the thing you measure. For the daily revenue table, it is minutes from midnight until the table lands.
The SLO is the target: ninety nine percent of days by six in the morning India time. That leaves an error budget of about three days a year.
Burn through it, say four late days by September, and the team stops shipping features until reliability work is done. The number ends the argument.

check.q: The team has used its whole error budget by September. What follows?
opts: Lower the SLO quietly
Reliability work comes before new features
Ignore it until next year
Add a new SLI
check.why: The point of an error budget is that spending it all pauses feature work in favour of reliability.

work: Write an SLI, SLO and budget for one critical table in a single line each.
Track late days against the budget on a team dashboard.

title: Finding and cutting the spend

beats.say: A team's warehouse bill hits forty thousand dollars. Where do you even start?
First, attribute. Tag every job and read the query logs, so each dollar belongs to a team, a table or a job. Then rank them. The top ten spenders are usually most of the bill.

Then pull four levers. Scan less, with partitions and only the columns you need. Compute cheaper, with spot nodes for batch jobs. Store less, with lifecycle rules that delete old files. Run less often: does that dashboard really need hourly refresh?

show.title: Four levers
items: Compute cheaper: spot nodes for batch
Run less often: question the freshness

beats.say: Moving one dashboard from hourly to daily cuts its runs from twenty four to one a day.

check.q: Which lever cuts cost by questioning the business need rather than the technology?
opts: Spot nodes
Partitioning
Running less often, such as hourly to daily
Compaction
check.why: Reducing refresh frequency removes work entirely. The other options make the same work cheaper.

work: Pull last month's query logs and list the ten most expensive queries or jobs.
Ask each dashboard owner whether hourly freshness is really needed.

title: Disaster recovery: RPO, RTO and the catch

beats.say: Your main region goes dark. Can you restore the pipelines, and how much data is gone?
Two numbers answer that. RPO is how much data you can lose, say fifteen minutes of events. RTO is how long until it works again, say four hours.
Copying files to a second region is the easy part. The catalog and orchestration state must be recoverable too. Without the table metadata and the job history, copied files are just a pile of bytes.
Most pipelines can be rebuilt by replaying raw data. Anything with no replayable source cannot, so protect it first. And rehearse the failover, because an untested plan is only a guess.

show.title: Recovery checklist
items: Rehearse the failover on a schedule

check.q: You replicate object storage to a second region. What is still missing for a real recovery?
opts: Nothing, the files are the data
Recoverable catalog and orchestration state, plus a rehearsal
A faster network
More dashboards
check.why: Without table metadata and job state, you cannot tell what the files mean or what to run. An untested failover may also fail.

work: Run a failover drill for one pipeline and record the real recovery time.
List every pipeline with no replayable source and decide how to protect it.

title: Cost traps that fool you

beats.say: Your costs rose twenty percent. Did the team get worse, or did the business grow?
Raw totals cannot tell you. Unit costs can: cost per terabyte processed, per dashboard, per trained model. If data grew thirty percent and cost rose twenty, efficiency actually improved.

Watch the traps. Untagged jobs land in a mystery bucket nobody owns. Spot nodes can be reclaimed in the middle of a job, so batch work must be safe to retry. And partitioning too finely creates thousands of tiny files, which makes queries slower and costlier.

check.q: Data volume grew 30% and total cost rose 20%. What is the fair conclusion?
opts: Efficiency got worse
Unit cost fell, so efficiency improved
Nothing can be concluded
Cost must be cut by 20%
check.why: Cost grew more slowly than the work done, so cost per unit fell.

work: Find the untagged share of your bill and assign owners.
Check that every spot-run batch job is safe to retry.

title: How much reliability to buy

beats.say: Should every dataset get five nines and a second region?

No. Each extra nine costs far more than the last, in standby capacity, duplicate storage and engineer time. Tier your datasets instead. A finance close table gets a tight target and a rehearsed failover. An internal experiment table gets a loose one.
Pick the recovery style by RPO and RTO. If four hours is fine, rebuild from replicated raw data in the second region. Only pay for a hot standby when minutes matter.
Let the business sign the targets. They are choosing how much risk to buy.

check.q: A table's RTO is four hours and raw data is replicated. What is the usual best-value recovery design?
opts: Hot standby in two regions
Rebuild in the second region from replicated raw data
No recovery plan
Manual copy by email
check.why: Rebuilding meets a four hour target at far lower standing cost. Hot standby is for minute-level needs.

work: Tier your datasets into three levels and attach an SLO to each tier.
Get the business owner of each Tier 1 table to sign its RPO and RTO.

title: Governing cost across many teams

beats.say: How do you cut cost across twenty teams without becoming the person who says no?
Make cost visible, not policed. Give each team a dashboard of its spend and unit cost, and let owners decide. Central mandates are slow; informed owners fix the waste themselves.
Spend your own time on the top ten spenders. Chasing the long tail of small jobs costs more engineer time than it saves.

Know when not to optimise. Saving two hundred dollars a month is a bad trade if it takes an engineer two weeks. Also count the hidden costs: cross region transfer, and the risk of cheaper but flakier nodes.

show.title: When not to optimise
items: Saving is smaller than the engineer time
Cheaper nodes that fail more often

check.q: Which approach scales best for cost control across many teams?
opts: A central team approves every query
Per-team visibility of spend and unit cost, with focus on the top spenders
Cut every budget by 10%
Ban spot nodes
check.why: Visibility lets owners act themselves, and focusing on the top spenders gives the largest savings for the effort.

work: Publish a per-team cost and unit cost view and review the top ten monthly.
Set a minimum saving, for example per engineer-week, before starting an optimisation.

title: The kitchen that never closes

beats.say: How do you move a restaurant kitchen without ever closing during dinner?
You don't. You build the new kitchen next door and keep cooking in the old one. For a while, both kitchens cook every order.
Each night, you taste the dishes side by side. If they match for two weeks straight, you send real orders to the new kitchen, one table at a time.
The old kitchen stays ready as a fallback, so a bad night means flipping back. Only when nobody orders from it do you lock the door. In data, this is called the strangler fig pattern.

chip.text: Delete the old only when nobody uses it

check.q: In the kitchen story, why keep the old kitchen running after the new one opens?
opts: So you can switch back quickly if the new one has problems
Because the new kitchen cannot cook without it
To double the number of dishes served
Because closing it is against the rules
check.why: The old kitchen is the fallback. Keeping it alive makes each move small and reversible, so a bad night costs little.

work: Name one system you would migrate and write down what would be its fallback.
Ask your team who still uses the old system today, and how you know.

title: Six steps of a safe migration

beats.say: You have four hundred Hive tables to move to Iceberg. Where do you even start?

show.sub: Hive tables to move to Iceberg

beats.say: Start with an inventory. List every table, job and consumer, using query logs to see who really reads what. Rank them by risk and dependency, so small leaf tables go first and the scary ones go last.
Next, build beside. New pipelines write new tables while the old ones keep running. Every day, reconcile: compare row counts, sums, and key-level diffs between old and new.

Cut over only when the gate passes, for example numbers match within tolerance for fourteen days in a row. Move one consumer group at a time, with a tested switch back. Finally, find remaining readers, announce dates, and delete.

check.q: Which is the best cutover criterion for a migrated table?
opts: The new pipeline has been running for a month
Numbers match within tolerance for 14 consecutive days
The engineer who built it feels confident
The old system is getting expensive
check.why: A measurable, repeatable reconciliation result is something others, even a Finance director, can verify and sign. Time or confidence alone proves nothing.

work: Pull query logs and rank your tables by how many consumers read them.
Write the cutover rule in your design doc as a number and a duration, not a feeling.

title: When matching counts still lie

beats.say: Your row counts match, so is the migration safe? Not yet.

Counts can match while content differs. A bad join might drop one row and duplicate another. Rounding can drift a sum. So also compare sums, and run key-level diffs that list keys missing on either side or with different values.

Then explain every difference. Some are bugs in the new system. Often they are bugs in the old one, which the business has trusted for years. Some are intended, like a new rule rejecting unknown cities. Write each down, with an owner, or the gate means nothing.
Rollback fails if untested. Keep the old pipeline running for a fixed window, and make sure a switch back works per table, without losing writes made on the new side.

chip.text: Untested rollback is not a rollback

check.q: Reconciliation shows a small set of keys whose values differ between old and new. What should you do first?
opts: Ignore it, since the row counts match
Overwrite the new table with the old values
Find out whether each difference is a new bug, an old bug, or intended, and record it
Extend the double run by a year
check.why: Differences are often old bugs or deliberate changes. Classifying and documenting each one keeps the cutover gate honest and gives owners something to approve.

work: Add a key-level diff to your reconciliation job, not only counts and sums.
Keep a log of every explained difference with a category and an owner.
Rehearse a rollback on one table before you need it.

title: The cost of doing it safely

beats.say: When is the right migration plan no migration at all?

show.sub: the cheapest table is the one you delete

beats.say: The double run is the big cost. Both systems bill you for months, plus engineers' time on reconciliation. Put that number in the design doc up front, or finance will find it for you, angrily.

A big bang cutover is shorter, but one surprise hits everyone at once and rollback is hard. Strangler fig costs more and takes longer, yet each step is small and reversible. Choose big bang only for small, low-risk, well-understood systems.

Run it on a calendar: announce, migrate, freeze, delete, with a named owner for each consumer group. Use the inventory to retire tables nobody reads rather than migrating them. Sign-off criteria like fourteen matching days let a Finance director say yes.

check.q: A small, low-risk internal table has one known reader and no downstream dependents. Which approach is most defensible?
opts: A months-long dual run with daily reconciliation
A direct cutover, since the blast radius is tiny
Never migrate it and keep it forever
Wait until all other tables are done
check.why: The strangler fig buys safety at the cost of a long double run. When the blast radius is tiny and the system is well understood, a direct cutover is cheaper and still safe.

work: Add a double-run cost line, with months and dollars, to your next migration design doc.
Use query logs to propose tables to retire instead of migrate.
Assign a named owner to every consumer group on the migration calendar.
